I added the torsion constraint to study.py and pushed it to GitHub as e8a7d65 on main of citgitfr/BenazzoVenkatadri_ThinShellSims. The design study is running; iteration 1 is in its buckling step in the background.

What the change adds - Torsion requirement: the study now checks that the tip twists no more than 1° under the 100 N·mm torque. - New loadcases step: after the failure check, each design is also run with the 100 N·mm torque and with the 50 N lateral tip load, and I check for material failure in both runs. - Screen estimate: the catalog screen now includes a torsional-stiffness estimate. It rules out every open section (tape spring, TRAC), leaving 4405 closed omega and corrugated designs. - Tested on iteration 1: the simulated twist was 0.95 times the screen estimate. - Bug fixed before the commit: the failure index for the torque and lateral runs was first being read from the coiling check. It now reads each run's own value. - I did not run the skill regression tests, because no skill scripts changed.

Iteration 1 (M55J/PAEK, [0/0/0], omega M006): - Twist is 0.031° under the torque, well under the 1° limit. - Failure indices are 1.9e-6 under the torque and 0.0083 under the lateral load. - The bending picture looks right, but the tip moved 1.48 mm under 25 N. That likely misses the 1 mm limit, in which case the buckling step skips itself. record will give the exact stiffness.

Interpretations to know - Buckling load: the 50 N lateral load is checked as a uniform 50,000 N·mm end moment, the cantilever's root moment, which is conservative. - Failure "throughout": failure is checked in the 25 N static run, the torque run and the 50 N lateral run. The nonlinear buckling path itself is not checked, because the buckling skill doesn't save the stresses along it. - CPU limit: each Abaqus job is capped at 8 CPUs under the shared-server rules, below your 16.

Updates: a status update fires every 15 minutes, but only while I'm between steps. It ends when this session closes and expires after 7 days. All study files are in Code for Project/11-17-26 (Tara)/boom_1m_lat50N_k25_tors1deg_hub100/.

Claude · 17:37

Iteration 1 is infeasible: the FE tip stiffness is 16.85 N/mm against the 25 N/mm required. Shear deformation explains the shortfall, so I added a shear term to the screen and the stiffness check, and pushed it as 4a91822.

Why the stiffness came out low: I split the FE deflection into a bending part and a shear part. - Bending: within 4.7% of beam theory. - Shear: 39% of the tip deflection. An all-0° laminate (M55J, 0.105 mm walls) has very low in-plane shear stiffness (G12 = 3.83 GPa), so this is real behaviour, not a modelling error.

What changed: - Screen estimate: the screen used bending only, so it overrated the stiffness of all-0° layups by about 1.7×. With the shear term, its estimate for iteration 1 is 0.91 of the FE result instead of 0.585. - Sanity check: the 15% beam-theory check now uses the same shear-corrected formula, so shear-soft designs are no longer falsely flagged. - Screen rerun: 3909 designs pass now (was 4405). Corrugated sections lead, with the lightest at about 0.076 kg. - Earlier result kept: iteration 1 stays in the ledger with its original flag and this explanation. The study folder's investigations/ has the deflection-split and patch scripts.

Claude · 17:50

The Abaqus check of iteration 1 finished, and its displacements match OpenSees. Tip deflection is −1.484 mm in Abaqus against −1.4835 mm in OpenSees, a 0.03% difference, and the tip rotation agrees to the same 0.03%. That confirms iteration 1 really is short on stiffness because of shear, and that the shear correction I added was the right call.

The ply-stress comparison does not match yet. The script's peak top-ply stresses differ by 74–88%: for example, fibre-direction stress is 10.3 MPa in Abaqus against 47.5 MPa in OpenSees. Each number is the largest value in its model, so the two may come from different spots, but I haven't confirmed that. An independent comparison agent is now checking both result files and will give a verdict, which I'll record before relying on this check.

Abaqus ran on 1 CPU, and its temporary folder under F:\Tara\abaqus_scratch was removed afterwards.

Iteration 2 (M30SC/PEEK [0/0/0], corrugated section C008) is still running its torque and lateral-load checks, then buckling. There is still no feasible design.

Claude · 17:52

Verification 1 is recorded as agree (1 of the minimum 5). The independent comparator found: - 81 of 82 checks within 3%. Tip deflection, curvatures, ply stresses and section forces all match to within 0.03–0.7%. - The one remaining difference is the in-plane rotation at the webs, which the two element types handle differently. Nothing downstream uses it. - The 74–88% stress mismatch in the Abaqus script's own quick check was a pairing error. It compared a web value with a flange value, and matched like for like they agree: 47.508 vs 47.510 MPa. That quick check lives in the opensees-to-abaqus skill, which I may only change with your OK, so I've noted it for the final report rather than fixing it.

Iteration 2 is now running its buckling step in the background. I'll record it when that finishes.

Three things you should know about it: - No buckling result. The study doesn't spend a buckling run on a design that already fails another constraint, so iteration 1 has no buckling number. - It carries a sanity flag. It was recorded before I added the shear correction, so its stiffness was compared with plain beam theory and flagged at −41.5%. The flag keeps it out of the best-design ranking and the screen calibration. Shear explains the flag, and the Abaqus match confirms the 16.85 N/mm stiffness is real. - Abaqus checked only the static case. It compared the 25 N tip-load run. The torque and lateral-load runs reuse the same model and mesh but were not compared in Abaqus; the study's verification step only exports the static case.

Step 2 is applying twice the end-rotation increment of step 1. The path is run under rotation control, so the load is not prescribed. The code doubles the step after an "easy" first step: step 1 took 9 iterations, and the code counts anything up to 11 as easy.

End rotation (rad) Moment (N·mm) Share of the 50,000 required
Step 1 (done) +0.000439 (total 0.000439) 6,523 (measured) 13%
Step 2 (attempting) +0.000878 (total 0.001316) ≈ +13,000 → ≈ 19,600 total (linear extrapolation, not measured) ≈ 39%
Requirement ≈ 0.0034 (extrapolated) 50,000 100%

Why it's taking so long: - Cost per iteration: step 1 took about 8 minutes for 9 Newton iterations, about 53 seconds per iteration on this roughly 140k-DOF corrugated mesh. - Step 2 has run 33 minutes, which is about 38 iterations at that rate. That is right at the 40-iteration limit per attempt, so this attempt is probably not converging. - What happens next: the solver will halve the step and retry at total rotation 0.00088 rad, about 13,000 N·mm.

A doubled step that won't converge, still at only about 40% of the requirement, could mean a local wall buckle is starting early. It could also just be the slow convergence this element type is known for. The log only prints when a step completes, so I can't tell which yet.

My recommendation stands: let it run, capped at about 2 hours total (until about 19:50). Now that the cost per iteration is clear, a sensible alternative is a cap of about 30 more minutes. That's enough to see whether the halved step converges, and an early non-convergence would itself be a warning sign about lateral buckling for this design.

Claude · 18:50

No, not for this run. More cores won't make this run faster without changing the buckling skill, and even then it wouldn't fix the real bottleneck.

Why extra cores don't help as things stand - The solver is single-threaded. The imperfect-path buckling run uses OpenSees' UmfPack sparse solver (shell_buckling.py:172). The process is using exactly one core: 20 CPU-seconds in 20 seconds, with 4 threads. - The path can't be split. Each load step starts from the converged state of the previous one, so the steps can't run side by side. - The existing parallel option doesn't apply. The skill's workers setting (up to 16) parallelises only the old step-A stability scan. The fast pipeline skips step A, so nothing here can use it.

What it would take, and why it's not worth it now - A multithreaded solver. Getting more cores into each iteration would mean switching that solver call to a multithreaded one such as MKL Pardiso, if your OpenSeesPy 3.8 build includes it. I haven't checked that. - Protocol steps. That is a skill change, so it needs your approval and a regression-test run before anything is committed. - The bottleneck is convergence, not speed. The doubled step failed after 40 iterations with its residual stuck at 0.0071 against a tolerance of 1e-6. The halved retry is already past the 9 iterations that step 1 needed. Faster iterations would only reach a "won't converge" answer sooner; they wouldn't make the step converge.

Using the idle cores for other designs - study.py runs one iteration at a time, and the protocol doesn't allow me to run the next design's skill scripts by hand outside it. - So I can't evaluate other designs in parallel without another study.py change.

If you want, after this study I can check whether Pardiso is available in your OpenSeesPy build. If it is, switching the solver could be a separate, regression-tested skill change.

Claude · 20:02

3518 of the 716,400 catalog combinations pass the new screen, out of the 3909 that passed before the buckling estimate was added. All 3518 are closed sections that the FE model can build.

The screen only rejects a design when an estimate misses a requirement by a wide margin. For buckling, it rejects below half the required 50,000 N·mm. So that number still includes designs expected to fail. A stricter subset is the designs whose calibrated estimates meet every requirement:

  • 1,197 are predicted feasible. 1,186 are corrugated and 11 are omega.
  • Almost all are 5-ply. 1,195 are 5-ply (0.175 mm) and only 2 are 4-ply; no 3-ply design is predicted to carry the lateral moment.
  • The lightest predicted-feasible design is 108.2 g. That is heavier than iterations 1–2 (66–76 g), which failed stiffness and buckling.

The rejections overlap, because one design can fail several checks:

Reason Designs rejected
Coiling on the hub (F_hub ≥ 1) 362,577
Stiffness estimate 348,286
Flattening the section (F_flat ≥ 1) 335,402
Torsion estimate 236,794
Buckling estimate (new) 187,053

The buckling estimate is fitted to perfect-shell linear buckling results. The imperfect-shell strength will be lower by an amount I don't know yet. Iteration 3 is the first buckling run that will calibrate this, and the predicted-feasible count may shrink once it does.

Iteration 3 (M55J/PAEK [0/45/0/45/0], omega M006, 110 g) is running its first steps in the background.

Claude · 20:52

Yes. The best fallbacks are 5-ply corrugated booms with 0/90 layups, at about 127–132 g, roughly 17–20 g heavier than iteration 4.

Why 0/90 layups. The screen's buckling estimate was fitted only to 0/90 layups, and within that range it matched 35 segment buckling analyses to within −18% to +17%. Iteration 4's [30/0/0/0/30] is an off-axis layup, so its estimate of 65,790 N·mm is an extrapolation. With 0/90 layups the estimate stays inside its fitted range. One data point already backs this up: the [0/90/0/90/0] M30SC/PEEK laminate on C008 buckled at 64,737 N·mm in a direct segment analysis.

I filtered the screen for 0/90 designs with at least 30% buckling margin, at least 3% calibrated stiffness margin, and a coiling index below 0.8. That leaves 22 designs. The most promising:

Design Mass Buckling estimate (needs 50,000) Stiffness (N/mm, needs 25) Coiling index on hub Why
T1100G/epoxy [90/0/0/0/90] on C008 131.9 g 83,835 N·mm (+68%) 36.9 0.67 Largest margins on both stiffness and buckling
M30SC/PEEK [90/0/0/0/90] on C008 126.9 g 67,070 N·mm (+34%) 28.5 0.27 Lightest of the 22, and an easy coil
T1100G/epoxy [90/0/0/0/90] on C005 131.8 g 75,394 N·mm (+51%) 32.5 0.38 Another section shape for the same material

Twist is under 0.01° for all of them, so torsion is not an issue.

Caveats - The buckling estimates are optimistic. They predict perfect-shell buckling, and the strength with the imperfection included will be lower by an amount we don't know yet. Iteration 4's run gives us the first measure of that gap. A large drop would rule out the +34% M30SC design, while the +68% T1100G design has more room. - Corrugated buckling runs are slow. C005 and C008 run buckling on their own 4.5 mm mesh. Iteration 2's C008 run took 85 minutes and stalled, so expect over an hour per design, longer near the limit. - M55J/PAEK is not in the list. With 0/90 layups on corrugated sections it fails a screen limit, most likely the coiling check on the corrugations' 9–12 mm radii.

If iteration 4 fails, my plan is to use its buckling result to recalibrate the buckling estimate, then pick T1100G/epoxy [90/0/0/0/90] on C008 for iteration 5. Its 68% buckling margin makes it the most likely to give the first feasible design.

Iteration 4's buckling run is progressing and is about three-quarters of the way to the pass level. There is still no feasible best design.

  • Step 2 converged at 43,013 N·mm at 20:48, in 12 iterations. That is 86% of the 50,000 N·mm requirement.
  • This laminate beats the seed's warning. The seed analysis predicted local buckling at 40,920 N·mm, but it used a stand-in laminate with 0/90 plies only; the real laminate has already carried more.
  • The structure is getting softer. Step 2 needed 12 iterations against 6 for step 1. So step 3 keeps the same step size instead of doubling, aiming at a total end rotation of about 0.00276 rad.
  • Step 3 has run for about 15 minutes. If the stiffness held, that rotation would correspond to about 71,700 N·mm, but the path is softening, so the moment reached will be lower. The pass level is 56,000 N·mm (1.12 × 50,000).
  • Three ways it can end:
  • Step 3 converges above 56,000 N·mm: iteration 4 passes buckling and becomes the first feasible design.
  • It peaks or stalls between 50,000 and 56,000 N·mm: a finer-mesh rerun starts automatically and decides.
  • It stalls below 50,000 N·mm: iteration 4 fails, and I move to the 0/90 corrugated fallbacks, starting with T1100G [90/0/0/0/90] on C008.

Good news on iteration 4: the failed step looks like slow convergence, not a buckle.

  • Step 3 nearly converged. It tried to reach 71,529 N·mm and stopped at the 40-iteration limit at 21:27. Its final residual was 4.8e-6, against a tolerance of 1e-6, so it ended about 5× off.
  • Why that matters: iteration 2's failed steps stopped about 7,000× off (residual 0.0071), meaning the structure was buckling. Here the structure was close to balanced even at 71,529 N·mm, so this points to slow convergence, not a buckle below that load.
  • Retry in progress: the solver halved the step at 21:27 and is now aiming for about 57,300 N·mm. That is above the 56,000 N·mm pass level (1.12 × 50,000) for this coarse mesh. If it converges there, the run passes buckling and stops.
  • Best design so far: none yet. Iteration 4 (110.0 g) passes every other requirement, so if this step converges it becomes the first feasible design. Its mesh-convergence check and an Abaqus verification come next.
  • Timing: each attempt costs about 1 minute per iteration, so the halved step should finish or fail by about 22:07 at the latest.

def final_B(idir, d):
    """Custom option buckling_objective 'A': method B (imperfect ASDShellQ4 path, mode A at 0.1 t) for the
    final design, so the report has the imperfect strength too. Range: 1.5 x A's critical end rotation /
    shortening, doubled while the path is still rising (up to 3 times)."""
    bc = jload(idir / 'buckling.json')
    if 'B_final_only' not in bc or d.get('buckling_B') is not None:
        return None
    mf = idir / 'buckling' / f'{bc["name"]}_mode.npz'
    if not mf.exists():
        return 'final B not run: no A mode file'

Yes. If iteration 4 is still the best design at the end, I will run its Abaqus verification. study.py finalize won't let the study close otherwise. It refuses until the best design has passed mesh convergence, has its own Abaqus verification, and at least 5 verifications have been requested in total; so far there is 1, of iteration 1.

For iteration 4, study.py verify 4 writes and checks two Abaqus scripts:

  1. Static run (25 N tip load). It is compared against the OpenSees model by the independent comparator agent, like iteration 1. It runs on 1 CPU and takes a few minutes.
  2. Buckling run. The design has a buckling result, so verify also writes an Abaqus script for the lateral-bending buckling case. That is the more important check here: OpenSees showed slow convergence on the path, and so far only the screen's shell-buckling fit stands behind it. That run is longer, a nonlinear Abaqus path rather than a few-second linear solve. Before using more than 1 CPU I'll ask you, and the shared-server cap is 8.

What verify does not cover is the torque and 50 N lateral-load runs. Those use the same model and mesh with different loads, so the static comparison checks the model itself. If you want them compared in Abaqus too, I can export the torsion run through the same opensees-to-abaqus skill as an extra check. That isn't something study.py does today, so I'd only do it with your OK.

As for timing: iteration 4 isn't due for verification yet, because verifications are spaced at least 5 iterations apart and the omega family was already verified at iteration 1. Its mesh convergence is running now. I'll verify it when the schedule calls for it or at the end, whichever comes first.

I've changed study.py so the final design's Abaqus verification must cover every OpenSeesPy load case, and pushed it to GitHub as 111116b on origin/main. It parses, but I haven't run it on a real design yet.

What changed - Final verification: study.py verify <i> --all-cases writes one Abaqus script per load case: the 25 N static case, the 100 N·mm torque, the 50 N lateral load, and the lateral-bending buckling case. It lists each script next to its OpenSees result. - One comparison per case: recording the verdict now needs a separate comparator report for each load case, so no case can be skipped. - Finalize enforces it: the study won't close until the best design has an all-cases verification. If that design already had a static-only check during the study, the all-cases one is added on top. - Mid-study checks stay static-only: those stay quick, because the buckling comparison is a nonlinear Abaqus run that takes much longer.

First real use will be the final design: running it now would spend a verification slot on iteration 4 before we know it's the winner. The comparator has only compared static runs so far, so I'll check how it handles the buckling case then. If it doesn't fit, I'll tell you rather than paper over it.

How the final verification will run - Order: the four Abaqus runs go one at a time through run_abaqus.py. - CPUs: 1 each for the static, torque and lateral runs. I'll ask before giving the buckling run more than 1 CPU, up to the 8-CPU server cap.

How many more iterations of the optimization do you anticipate running?

Claude · 22:14

Probably about 15 more, if the study follows its stopping rules. Fewer if you decide to end it early, and there is a reasonable case for that.

Stopping rules in study.py - Stop if the best design has improved by less than 1% over the last 15 iterations. This only applies from iteration 20 on. - Stop if no untried candidate is left, or none is predicted feasible. - Stop at 100 iterations, a hard limit. - The second rule won't fire soon: there are about 1,190 predicted-feasible candidates, almost all heavier than iteration 4. So the first point the study can recommend stopping is iteration 20, 15 iterations from now.

What those 15 iterations would likely achieve - Only 2 untried designs are both lighter than iteration 4 (110.0 g) and predicted feasible: iteration 5 (108.2 g, running now) and its mirror-image layup [−30/0/0/−30], which should behave the same. - The other 611 lighter designs are predicted to fail, mostly on stiffness (about 21–23 N/mm against 25). - After iterations 5 and 6, the remaining iterations would test heavier designs. They would sharpen the calibration but are unlikely to beat the best design. The exception is if the buckling estimate turns out to be conservative for some family. Iteration 4's real buckling strength is at least 57,331 N·mm against an estimate of 65,790, so there's no sign of that so far.

Cost

Item Estimate
Each omega iteration ~1 h
Each corrugated iteration 1–2 h or more (full-mesh buckling run)
15 more iterations roughly 15–25 h of compute
4 more Abaqus verifications (minimum 5) a few minutes each, except the final all-cases check
Final all-cases buckling run in Abaqus ≈ several hours, my guess

My recommendation 1. Finish iteration 5. If it passes, run its mirror layup as iteration 6 to confirm. 2. Run the remaining Abaqus verifications: the final design with all load cases, plus three more designs that differ from it. 3. Then end the study with finalize --force-reason. The early end and its reason would be stated in the report: no lighter design is predicted feasible.

That is about 1–2 more iterations and roughly 4–8 hours, most of it the Abaqus buckling check. The alternative is to let it run to iteration 20 under the rules, about 15 more iterations and 15–25+ hours. Ending before iteration 20 needs your explicit OK, because it overrides the study's own stopping rule.

The lightest of these is 105.5 g (T1100G on C008), about 4% below iteration 4.

Plan for iterations 5–20: one probe per family, taking the design closest to passing.

  1. Iteration 5 (running now): M55J [30/0/0/30] on C005. The estimate is +3% over the requirement, so this directly tests the off-axis 4-ply corrugated case.
  2. C008: T1100G [60/0/0/60], 105.5 g, estimate −6%. C008 is the largest family.
  3. M022 omega: M55J [0/0/0/0/0], 106.1 g, estimate −8%. An all-0° laminate sits inside the range the estimate was fitted on, so this tests whether the fit holds for the omega shape.
  4. C006 and C007: their closest designs.
  5. Then follow the results. - Any family whose real strength exceeds its estimate gets probed lighter and with other layups. - Families where the estimate holds get no further runs.

Throughout, mirror-image layups count as one design, the lightest feasible design so far stays the best, and the Abaqus verifications are scheduled along the way.

How the result shows up: a design that fails buckling gives its true peak (or stall) moment. study.py stores the ratio of measured to estimated strength for each section family and uses it to rescale that family's estimates. If a family proves conservative, more of its designs become predicted feasible on their own, without any manual edits.

I'll cite your request and the FE results as they come in. - Each corrugated probe takes 1–2 hours, because buckling runs on the full design mesh. Iteration 6 is the new best design: T1100G/epoxy [60/0/0/60] on corrugated section C008, at 104.9 g, about 2.6% lighter than iteration 5's 107.7 g. It passes every requirement. It finished before the original 01:56 cap, so the cap extension wasn't needed and I cancelled that check.

On your question about the buckling estimate: for the C008 corrugated family it is pessimistic. The screen predicted this design would fail buckling at 47,053 N·mm, but the simulation carried at least 52,210 N·mm. So the estimate was at least 11% low here. The run stops once it passes the 50,000 N·mm requirement, so I don't know how much higher the true strength is.

That opens up more of the C008 family. About 74 designs in it weigh less than iteration 5 and failed the screen only on its buckling estimate.

The study only adjusts its estimate when a buckling run ends at a real peak or stall. Runs that stop by design above the requirement give only a lower bound, so the screen won't update by itself. I'll therefore keep choosing C008 designs, citing iteration 6's result as the reason for overriding the screen.

Running now, one after the other: 1. Mesh convergence of iteration 6. 2. Abaqus verification of iteration 6, the study's first on a corrugated section. Static case on 1 CPU.

After those, iteration 7 will try a lighter C008 design whose estimated buckling shortfall is around 10%. Iteration 6's margin shows estimates up to about 11% low are worth testing.

How does the fact that iteration 6 passed change the plan for the family probes?

Claude · 07:05

Iteration 6 passing changes the plan's goal more than its method. The best design is now 104.9 g, so a probe only matters if it could beat that. That removes most of the original list and leaves one realistic candidate, iteration 7, which is running now.

The original probes and where they stand

Planned probe Mass Status now
C008: T1100G [60/0/0/60] 105.5 g screened, 104.9 g actual Done (iteration 6): passed, new best
M022 omega: M55J [0/0/0/0/0] 106.1 g Heavier than the best, so it can't win; would only calibrate
C006 / C007: closest designs about 105–107 g Same: heavier, calibration only

What still could beat 104.9 g. There are 137 untried designs lighter than the best: - 124 fail the stiffness estimate. That estimate has proven accurate (FE/estimate 0.95–0.97 across 5 runs), so these designs genuinely are too soft. A conservative buckling estimate can't rescue them. - 13 meet stiffness. Only 1 of them, iteration 7 (IM7 [45/0/0/45] on C008, 102.8 g), is within 15% of the buckling requirement. The other 12 are 42% or more short, which would need the estimate to be about 1.7× too low. Nothing seen so far suggests anything near that.

So the binding constraint for lighter booms has moved from buckling to bending stiffness. Your question about whether some family's buckling estimate is conservative now comes down to iteration 7: - If it passes, the C008 estimate is at least 15% conservative and the best design drops to 102.8 g. - If it fails, its stall load gives the first actual buckling strength for C008. That tells us how conservative the estimate really is: iteration 6 only shows it is at least 11% low, because its run stopped once it passed the requirement.

After iteration 7, about 13 iterations remain before iteration 20. I don't expect any of them to find a lighter feasible boom from this catalog. Options: 1. Calibration probes: one heavier design per untested family (M022, C006, C007, C005 0/90) to measure how far off the estimate is for each. This doesn't reduce mass, but it gives the report a calibration table per family. 2. Close out: use the remaining work for the 3 more Abaqus verifications still required (minimum 5). That includes the all-load-case check of the final design you asked for, whose Abaqus buckling run is long. Then finalize before iteration 20; that needs your explicit OK. 3. A mix: two or three calibration probes, then close out.

Claude · 07:09

No. Apart from the trivially balanced all-0° iterations 1–2, every design so far has been unbalanced. A balanced off-axis laminate also can't beat the current best in this catalog: they all run about 22–27 g heavier than iteration 6.

Why they are heavy. The layup catalog has only symmetric 3–5 ply layups that each include at least one 0° ply. A balanced off-axis layup needs a +θ and −θ pair on each side of the mid-plane, plus the 0°, which takes 5 plies. Only 6 such layups exist:

Layups Mirror images
[30/−30/0/−30/30] [−30/30/0/30/−30]
[45/−45/0/−45/45] [−45/45/0/45/−45]
[60/−60/0/−60/60] [−60/60/0/60/−60]

At 5 plies (0.175 mm), any design using them is heavy: - 40 balanced off-axis designs pass the screen. The lightest is L038 [30/−30/0/−30/30] on C005 at 126.8 g, but it falls short on stiffness (21.8 N/mm against 25). - 16 are predicted feasible. The lightest is T1100G (L011) [30/−30/0/−30/30] on C005 at 131.8 g: stiffness 28.5 N/mm, buckling estimate 59,570 N·mm, hub coiling index 0.86. - For comparison, iteration 6 is 104.9 g, so the lightest feasible balanced design is about 26% heavier.

Why balance might still matter to you. The unbalanced 4-ply designs (iterations 5–7) have stretch–shear and bend–twist coupling. - In the simulations: the FE models include these couplings fully, and the stiffness, torsion, failure and buckling checks all passed with them. The tip load produces a slight twist, visible in iteration 5's picture. - Not checked: two practical effects outside what this study simulates. - Coupled laminates can twist during coiling and deployment. - Curing and temperature changes cause in-plane shear distortion. - Your requirements didn't ask for balance, so the study hasn't penalised coupling.

If you want a balanced laminate, I can add that restriction to the requirements and re-screen the catalog. The best design would then likely be about 132 g, probably T1100G [30/−30/0/−30/30] on C005. Alternatively, with the iterations left before 20, I can run one balanced design as a comparison point so the report shows what balance costs in mass. Iteration 7's buckling run continues either way.

The short answer: no. There are 13 iterations left before iteration 20 (8–20), and only about 8 of them answer a real open question. Adding the balanced run takes one of the leftover filler slots, not a probe.

The stiffness side is already settled. FE stiffness has matched the screen's estimate within 0.953–0.973 over five runs. So the four lighter designs that miss stiffness by 2.6–5.6% really do fail, and nothing lighter than 104.9 g can be rescued that way. Buckling is the only open question.

Plan for iterations 8–20

Iteration Design Purpose
7 (running) IM7 [45/0/0/45] on C008, 102.8 g, buckling estimate −13% Last realistic chance at a lighter boom
8 Depends on 7 If 7 passes: mesh-convergence check and a mirror-layup check of the new best. If it fails: its stall moment is the first measured C008 buckling strength.
9 M22 omega, M55J [0/0/0/0/0], 106.1 g, estimate −8% Calibrate the omega family; cheap, since its buckling run uses the 4 mm coarse mesh
10 C005 with a 0/90 layup Calibrate corrugated designs inside the range the buckling estimate was fitted to
11 C006, closest design Calibrate a family not yet tested
12 C007, closest design Calibrate a family not yet tested
13 Balanced: T1100G [30/−30/0/−30/30] on C005, about 132 g Show what a balanced laminate costs in mass
14–15 Same [60/0/0/60] layup on C008 with other materials (L030, L002, about 106 g, estimates −5/−6%) Check that iteration 6's "estimate is at least 11% conservative" holds across materials
16–17 One design per family with an estimate about 20–30% short These should buckle before the cutoff and give a real buckling strength, not a lower bound (see below)
18–20 Follow the data More runs on any family that shows real conservatism; otherwise mirror-layup checks of the best

Iterations 16–17 are there because a run that passes its cutoff only gives a lower bound, so iterations 4–6 never measured how conservative the estimate actually is. A design meant to fall short peaks before the cutoff and reveals its true strength. study.py uses those values to recalibrate each family automatically.

Abaqus verifications: 2 of the minimum 5 are done (iterations 1 and 6). The other 3: - Iteration 4, the best omega design: a second check of the omega family, on a 5-ply laminate. - One calibration probe, probably a C005 or M22 run. - The final best design with all load cases (static, torque, lateral and buckling), as you asked. Its Abaqus buckling run is long, and I'll ask you before using more than 1 CPU for it.

Timeline: roughly 13 × 1–2 h, about 15–25 h of runs, plus the final Abaqus buckling run, so probably 1–1.5 days. Overnight the session paused for about 5.5 h, so expect similar gaps if the machine sleeps.

What is iteration 8?

Claude · 09:54

You've caught a gap in my updates: I've been saying "then iteration 9" without naming iteration 8. The mesh-convergence check I mentioned isn't an iteration; it's a separate rerun of the best design and uses no iteration slot. So iteration 8 depends on how iteration 7 ends:

  • If iteration 7 passes (new best at 102.8 g): iteration 8 is the mirror layup, IM7 [−45/0/0/−45] on C008, same mass.
  • Why it matters: these 4-ply layups are unbalanced, so they couple bending and twisting, and lateral buckling isn't necessarily symmetric in the sign of the off-axis plies.
  • What it settles: if the final design is going to hinge on a 1–2% buckling margin, I want to know whether flipping +45° to −45° changes that margin, since it could pass one way and fail the other.
  • Effect on the plan: the M022 omega probe stays at iteration 9, and the rest of the plan stays as saved.
  • If iteration 7 fails: its stall load gives the C008 calibration with no extra run. Iteration 8 then becomes the M22 omega calibration probe, everything else moves up one, and one free slot opens at the end. I'd fill that with one more design meant to buckle well below the requirement, so it measures a real buckling strength.

I'll update investigations/PLAN_iterations_8-20.md so it numbers iteration 8 explicitly. In the status updates I'll stop calling the convergence check an iteration step.

Claude · 11:21

Within the catalog, there is one long shot left. It is worth one iteration because it would also measure the true strength of the C008 family.

Lighter designs still untried: 43 designs are lighter than 102.2 g. - 38 fail stiffness. The stiffness estimate has matched the FE runs within 0.953–0.977 over 6 runs, so they really are too soft. They're out. - 5 pass stiffness, and all of them fall far short on the buckling estimate:

Design Mass Buckling estimate Shortfall
M55J [30/0/30] on C008 (and its mirror) 81.2 g (−21%) 28,803 N·mm 42% short
M55J [30/0/30] on C006 (and its mirror) 81.1 g 27,108 N·mm 46% short
M30SC [0/0/0/0] on C008 101.5 g 26,540 N·mm 47% short

The long shot: M55J [30/0/30] on C008, 81.2 g. - To pass, the buckling estimate would have to be about 1.7× too low for this design. - So far we only know it is at least 1.17× too low on C008, from iteration 7 (at least 51,014 N·mm measured vs 43,644 estimated). Every C008 run stopped once it passed the requirement, so the true margin is unknown and could be larger. - Against it: the 3-ply all-0° C008 of iteration 2 buckled at about 12,700 N·mm, close to its own estimate. That's a different layup, but it suggests 3-ply C008 walls stay weak. - So passing is unlikely but not ruled out. The payoff is about a 21% lighter boom. - Even if it fails, the buckling run should stop at a real peak below the requirement. That gives the first actual buckling strength of an off-axis C008 design, which is what the iteration 16–17 calibration probes in the plan were meant to provide. I'd suggest running it as iteration 9 and moving the M22 omega probe back one slot. Cost is about 1–2 h.

Beyond the catalog: the study can only pick from the existing catalogs. To go lighter otherwise, the catalog would need to grow, and catalog changes go through the CompositeLaminaLibrarian agent, only at your request. Possible directions: - Geometry: corrugated sections between C008 and its neighbours, or with more lobes or smaller radii, giving more bending stiffness per gram. - Layups: for example 4-ply [θ/0/0/θ] with other angles. The catalog only has 0, ±30, ±45, ±60 and 90. - Thinner plies: every material in the catalog uses 0.035 mm plies.

Each would need a re-screen and new runs. Continuous geometry optimisation exists only for the CTM omega family, not for corrugated sections.

Recommendation: run the 81 g M55J design as iteration 9, and keep the catalog unchanged unless you want to extend it.

Claude · 13:07

Iteration 4 is Abaqus-verified, and the comparator agent's verdict is agree. That is the second omega section and the third verification overall; the study needs at least 5.

  • What matches: displacements, tip rotations, curvatures, flange ply stresses and section forces agree within about 0.1–1%. In the middle of the boom (30–970 mm), flange stresses agree within 0.8% of peak.
  • What differs: all 68 flagged differences fall into three groups, none in the region that decides the design:
  • within 15 mm of either end, at the clamp or the rigid tip;
  • the very small stresses in the 2-element-wide web;
  • the in-plane (drilling) rotation, which the two element types handle differently.
  • No sign errors: the agent found no sign, factor-of-two, ply-order or boundary-condition error. Every scale factor is between 0.95 and 1.02.
  • Quick stress check in the Abaqus results file: it disagreed for the third time, and it is a flaw in that check, not in the model. It compares a point that exists only in the web laminate with the flange's top ply. The full comparison pairs them correctly: flange top ply 13.06 vs 13.12 MPa. The check lives in the opensees-to-abaqus skill, so I haven't touched it; fixing it needs your OK, and I'll list it as a known issue in the final report.

The agent wrote one scratch script outside the project folder, in the session's temporary scratchpad. Nothing was changed in the project apart from the comparison report and its plots in the iteration 4 folder.

Three Abaqus verification records had been lost because of a bug in study.py. I fixed the bug, restored the records, and pushed the fix to GitHub as 8197b2d. Iteration 9 is now running.

Iteration 8 passes. The mirrored layup, IM7 [−45/0/0/−45] on C008, reached at least 50,219 N·mm in buckling, against 50,000 required. The run stops once it passes, so the true limit may be higher. It weighs 102.2 g, the same as iteration 7, so it doesn't change the best design. Its buckling margin is thinner than iteration 7's (≥51,014 N·mm): the two layups behaved identically until the last load step. So the best design's buckling margin is real but only 0.4–2% above the requirement. The final Abaqus buckling check of the best design, which you asked to include all load cases, is the independent test of that.

The bug. A buckling run can take hours. It read the study's state file when it started and wrote that old copy back when it finished. Any verification result recorded in between was overwritten. That happened to: - iteration 1's verdict, - iteration 6's verdict, - iteration 4's whole verification record.

Fix and restore. - Fix: study.py now re-reads the state file before saving, both after each run step and after a mesh-convergence rerun. - Restore: I re-recorded all three as "agree" from the comparator reports already on disk, with a note on each. - Rest of the state: mesh convergence, calibration, ledger and designs are all intact. - Count: 3 of the minimum 5 verifications are on record.

Now running. Iteration 9 is the long-shot design: M55J [30/0/30] on C008, 81.2 g. Its first steps are running. I cancelled the 16:15 check because iteration 8 has finished.

The best design is still iteration 7, IM7 [45/0/0/45] on C008, at 102.2 g.

Claude · 18:26

Iteration 9, the 81.2 g M55J [30/0/30] boom on C008, is stopped and recorded as a buckling failure. Its strength is about half the 50,000 N·mm requirement.

Buckling result

Load (N·mm) Outcome
21,670 converged
36,102 ran away, residual 0.154: clear instability
28,809 did not converge, residual 8.7e-5
25,269 converged (last converged load)
  • Strength: between 25,269 and 28,809 N·mm.
  • Everything else passes: stiffness 27.84 N/mm (FE is 0.98 of beam theory), twist 0.0029°, failure index at most 0.76.

What this means for the C008 buckling estimate. It is not uniformly conservative; how good it is depends on the laminate:

Design Screen estimate (N·mm) FE result (N·mm) Estimate vs FE
4-ply [±45/0/0/±45], iterations 7–8 43,644 ≥ 50,219–51,014 at least 15–17% low
4-ply [60/0/0/60], iteration 6 47,053 ≥ 52,210 at least 11% low
3-ply [30/0/30], iteration 9 28,803 25,269–28,809 about right to 14% high

So the thin 3-ply walls get none of the extra margin the 4-ply designs showed. No lighter C008 design comes close to working, and iteration 7 (102.2 g) is very likely the lightest feasible boom in this catalog.

Running now: iteration 10, the omega M022 calibration probe: M55J [0/0/0/0/0] on M022, 106.1 g, buckling estimate 8% short. - That laminate is within the range the buckling estimate was fitted on, so this tests the fit directly on an omega section. - The omega's buckling run uses the 4 mm coarse mesh, so it should be quicker than the corrugated runs. - Its laminate, model and plot steps are running now.

Best design: iteration 7, IM7 [45/0/0/45] on C008, 102.2 g. Three of the required five Abaqus verifications are recorded.

Iteration 10 gave no buckling data. Its stiffness came out at 24.57 N/mm, 1.7% under the 25 N/mm requirement, so the study skipped its buckling run as designed. It passed everything else: failure index 0.16, twist 0.019°, hub coiling index 0.20.

Its recorded sanity flag was a false alarm. study.py compared it against iteration 1's stiffness ratio, which was computed before I added shear deformation to beam theory. I recomputed that reference with the shear-corrected formula: 0.585 became 0.913. Iteration 10's ratio of 0.923 is within 1% of it. The change is logged in the study's state file.

Iteration 11 replaces it as the omega calibration probe: M55J [0/0/0/0/0] on omega M006, 110.0 g. - Stiffness: estimated about 20% above the requirement, so the buckling run will happen this time. - Buckling: the screen estimate is 40,505 N·mm, about 19% below the 50,000 required. The run should therefore peak below the requirement, giving the first measured buckling strength for an omega section. - Status: its first steps are running now.

The best design is still iteration 7: IM7 [45/0/0/45] on C008, 102.2 g.

Claude · 18:43

I've plotted iteration 7 (IM7 [45/0/0/45] on C008) in its lateral-bending buckling case, with one caveat: these are not snapshots from the buckling run itself. study.py's buckling run keeps only its load–rotation history and the seed mode, not the deformed boom. So the two plots are rebuilt as follows.

1. Deformed boom at 51,014 N·mm (it007_lateral_moment_deformed.png) - How it was made: a linear solve of the iteration-7 model under the end moment where the buckling run stopped. - Why that's a fair stand-in: the buckling run's response was still linear at that point. Tip rotation here is 0.003839 rad, against 0.003825 rad from the buckling run, a 0.4% difference. - What it shows: smooth lateral bending, with a maximum displacement of 1.92 mm (drawn ×52) and a peak failure index of 0.0016. - What it can't show: the growth of the 0.1 t imperfection right near the buckling limit.

2. Buckling mode used as the imperfection seed (it007_buckling_seed_mode.png) - Where the buckling is: confined to the flat bonded tab on the +y side of the corrugated section (about 0° in the unrolled map, y ≈ 60–80 mm in the cross-section). The tab's free edge ripples out of plane. - Pattern along the boom: the ripple repeats about every 72 mm, the length of the segment the mode was computed on, tiled over the full 1 m. - Why that side: a +z end moment puts the +y side in compression. The tab sticks out with a free edge, so it is the section's weakest element in compression. That is consistent with the boom carrying more lateral moment as its laminate gets stiffer. - Caveat: for this off-axis layup the seed shape comes from a substitute laminate with only 0° and 90° plies, as the protocol allows. The strength itself came from the true laminate.

That free tab is what limits lateral buckling for C008. It's useful to know for the report, and for any future catalog work on tab geometry, which I won't do unless you ask.

The plots and the script that makes them (investigations/it007_buckling_plots.py) are in the study's investigations folder. Iteration 11 is still running its load cases.

Claude · 23:03

Iteration 12 is now Abaqus-verified with an agree verdict, the second check of a corrugated section and the 4th verification overall (at least 5 are required).

  • Abaqus matches the stiffness that raised the flag: tip deflection is −0.70424 mm in OpenSees and −0.70513 mm in Abaqus, a 0.13% difference.
  • The flag isn't a modelling error: iteration 12's stiffness came out at 0.916 of the shear-corrected beam-theory value. Abaqus reproduces it, so it's real behaviour of an all-0° laminate, whose low in-plane shear stiffness makes the simple shear estimate less accurate. All three all-0° designs so far (iterations 1, 11 and 12) give 0.913–0.916.
  • Overall agreement: flange ply stresses agree within 0.09%, section forces within 0.01–0.44%, and curvatures within 0.55%.
  • Flagged differences: 36 checks are flagged, all at the boom ends, in the web's in-plane rotation (which the two codes treat differently), or in very small web stresses. The results file's quick stress check again compares a web stress with a flange stress, so its −85% gap is a false alarm.
  • Housekeeping: the comparator kept its scratch script in the iteration folder, as asked, and changed no tools.

Iteration 13 (balanced) Iteration 7 (best, unbalanced)

Mass 131.3 g 102.2 g
Buckling at least 66,551 N·mm (+33% margin) about +2% margin
  • Why it's heavier: the only balanced off-axis layups in the catalog are 5-ply.

Claude · 14:18

Iteration 19 is stopped under your 2-hour rule and recorded as a buckling failure. - Result: IM7/8551-7 [0/30/30/0] on C005 buckles at 25,775–32,110 N·mm, short of the 50,000 N·mm requirement. - Against the screen: that is 0.85–1.05× the screen's raw estimate of 30,488 N·mm, so the estimate is about right here.

What the extra margin seems to depend on: across the measured runs, the 1.25–1.37× extra buckling margin shows up when the angled plies are on the outer faces.

Run Layup Section Measured / raw estimate
16 [30/0/0/30] C008 1.26–1.37×
17 [60/0/0/60] C006 1.25–1.27×
18 [30/0/0/30] C007 0.93–1.11×
19 [0/30/30/0] C005 0.85–1.05×
  • C007 looks like an exception: it has the angled plies outside but no extra margin.
  • Plies inside: iteration 19 puts them in the middle and also gets no extra margin.
  • What this means: the margin seems to depend on both the corrugation shape and where the angled plies sit. It is not one factor for the whole corrugated family.

Iteration 20, the last one, is running: M55J [0/0/45/0/0] on omega section M006, 110.0 g. It should give a real buckling strength for an omega with angled plies; the previous omega run (iteration 4) passed, so it only gave a lower bound.

After iteration 20: - Final check: an Abaqus check of the best design (iteration 7) with every load case, as you asked: 25 N static, torque, 50 N lateral and buckling. That makes 5 verifications. - Close-out: finalize the study, write the report and commit. I'll ask you before using more than 1 CPU for the Abaqus buckling run.

Best design: iteration 7, IM7 [45/0/0/45] on C008, 102.2 g.

The push still fails with the same GitHub message:

remote: You must set up two-factor authentication (2FA) on your account, with only the methods allowed by this repository's owner.
error: 403

Git on this machine authenticates through Git Credential Manager, which is still sending the login it saved before you turned on 2FA. GitHub keeps rejecting that saved login. Your account now needs a fresh sign-in, through the browser or a new personal access token. I can't do that for you: - The sign-in is interactive: it opens a browser window and needs you. - Clearing the saved login means changing your Windows credentials, which is outside the project folder and isn't mine to touch.

To fix it, from a terminal in the repo folder: 1. Open Windows Credential Manager → Windows Credentials and remove the entry git:https://github.com. You can also remove it from the command line:

printf "protocol=https\nhost=github.com\n\n" | git credential-manager erase
  1. Push again. Git Credential Manager will open a browser to sign in to GitHub, including the 2FA step:
git push origin main

If your organisation's 2FA rule also requires a specific method (an authenticator app or a passkey rather than SMS), check that the method you set up is one it allows. The message says "only the methods allowed by this repository's owner".

Claude · 14:44

The Abaqus buckling check of the best design, iteration 7, has finished, and it raises the most important question of the study:

Method (Abaqus, 8 CPUs) Lateral moment (N·mm) vs 50,000 requirement
Linear buckling analysis (LBA), mode 1 (perfect shell) 49,457 −1.1%
Preloaded eigenvalue, f = 0.50 / 0.80 / 0.95 48,786 / 48,510 / 48,445 −2.4 to −3.1%
Riks imperfect path rises linearly to 102,050 with no peak or softening +104%
OpenSees imperfect path B (study result) passed ≥ 51,014 +2.0%

What it means: - The two codes agree closely on where buckling starts. Abaqus puts the first buckling mode at 48,400–49,500 N·mm. That is within 3–5% of where the OpenSees run had trouble converging (failed attempts at 51,000–58,800, success at 51,014). Iteration 7's seed mode is the flat bonded tab on the compressed side rippling locally. - That local buckling starts about 1–3% below the requirement. Under a strict reading of "does not buckle", iteration 7 fails by a hair. - But the boom does not collapse there. Abaqus Riks carries the load linearly to twice the requirement, and the OpenSees path also kept going past 50,000. A flat plate rippling locally keeps carrying load after it buckles, so its strength exceeds its buckling load. - One caveat on the Riks run: it shows no softening at all, so it may not have picked up the local mode. Treat it as consistent with the boom holding, not as proof.

So whether iteration 7 meets the requirement depends on what "does not buckle" means. The study so far has used the protocol's definition, the imperfect load-carrying path. A stricter reading, no local buckling at all below 50,000 N·mm, makes iteration 7 fail by about 1%. The other designs that only just passed in OpenSees (iterations 5, 6, 8, 14, 15 at 50,000–52,000) would then also be in doubt. The comfortable passes, iteration 4 (≥ 57,331) and the balanced iteration 13 (≥ 66,551), would be safer choices.

The study is finished: iteration 6 (104.9 g) is the final design, and iteration 20 has been recorded as a buckling failure.

Iteration 20 (omega section M006, layup [0/0/45/0/0], 110.0 g): I stopped it at the two-hour check under your rule. - The last converged load was 27,391 N·mm, and nothing had converged after 15:42. An attempt at 41,014 N·mm failed to converge, and one at 54,755 N·mm failed badly. - That puts its buckling strength between 27,391 and 41,014 N·mm, against a design estimate of 45,197 N·mm. - So for omega sections the estimate is about 40% too high, the same as iteration 11.

Stopping the run also ended the study.py wrapper before it marked the buckling step as failed. I set that by hand and logged the edit in the state notes, then recorded iteration 20 and ran study.py finalize.

Final design: iteration 6, material L011, layup [60/0/0/60], section C008 (closed corrugated boom), 104.9 g.

Requirement Result Limit
Stiffness under 25 N tip load 27.81 N/mm ≥ 25 N/mm (+11%)
Buckling, OpenSees path ≥ 52,210 N·mm (lower bound; run stopped at the cutoff, still rising) ≥ 50,000 N·mm
Buckling, first in Abaqus 55,436–56,397 N·mm > 50,000 N·mm (+11–13%)
Tip twist under 100 N·mm torque 0.0037° ≤ 1°
Hashin failure index (under 1 = no failure): bending / coiled on hub / lateral 50 N / torque 0.38 / 0.45 / 0.0015 / ~0 < 1
  • Abaqus agrees on every load case (static, torsion, lateral and buckling), and mesh convergence passed.
  • Iterations 7 and 8 (102.2 g) are lighter, but both fail the strict buckling criterion in Abaqus, at 1.1–3.1% below 50,000 N·mm.

REPORT.md is complete: - the final design and the strict buckling criterion - the history of all 20 iterations - a table of how the buckling estimate compares with the simulations, by section family - all 8 Abaqus verifications - limitations, including every hand edit to the study state

On your question about the buckling estimate: - Conservative for C008 and C006 sections with angled outer plies, by at least 9–17%. That extra margin couldn't be used, because a local buckle appears just below 50,000 N·mm on the lighter designs. - About 40% too high for omega sections.

The commit would include only the five paths finalize listed (requirements.json, constraints.json, ledger.csv, REPORT.md and final/).

Claude · 17:06

The narrative report is done, and everything from the session is committed and pushed to GitHub.

Report: NARRATIVE_REPORT.pdf, 11 pages. I checked its layout through a rendered copy of the HTML version, which shares its content and styling. It covers: 1. What you asked for: every load case, how each was modelled, its pass condition, and the decisions you made along the way. 2. Tool changes: torsion, the shear (Timoshenko) term, the fix for unbalanced layups, and the closed-section buckling fit. 3. Pre-screen: all 716,400 combinations, broken down by section family. - Open sections were ruled out by torsion alone. The best tape spring reaches only 0.24% of the required torsional stiffness and the best TRAC 0.86%, so they would twist about 410° and 120° instead of 1°. - Tape springs also fail the stiffness and buckling estimates everywhere. 4. Path through the iterations: in four phases, with a table giving each iteration's design, why it was chosen and its outcome. 5. Abaqus verifications: when each of the 7 checks was run, why then, and what it showed. The main lesson is that the OpenSees buckling path can pass a design whose first buckling is below the requirement; that is what led to the strict criterion. 6. Buckling-estimate accuracy: how the estimate compared with the simulations, by family. 7. Why no untested design can win: every catalog design was re-checked using the most optimistic stiffness and buckling corrections measured in the study. - 69,437 designs are heavier than iteration 6. - Of the 646,963 lighter ones, only 9 pass every optimistic check. Four are iterations 7, 8 and 17 or the mirror of iteration 17; the rest fail stiffness or are 0.03 g heavier. - One real gap remains: the untested L006 [±60/0/0/±60] C008 pair (102.8 g on the screen's mass formula). With the stiffness correction measured for that layup on C008, it misses stiffness by 1.1%. That is a prediction; only an FE run would confirm it. 8. Limitations.

Figures: the screen breakdown, the iteration path, mass vs stiffness and mass vs buckling (each with a zoomed panel showing where untested designs sit), the buckling calibration, and the final design. The scripts that make the plots and the PDF are in investigations/.

GitHub: two commits, 209fa44 (the full study folder and the Running Log entry, about 1.9 GB as you chose) and the report commit. The local folder matches GitHub, apart from the Abaqus ODB files, which are git-ignored.
